sentences.text: Tropeognathus possessed distinctively convex, keeled crests on the tip of its upper snout and a smaller mass on the underside of its lower jaws.

The upper crest extended from the snout tip back to the large opening on the side of the skull, giving the animal a broader skull than its relatives because the upper jaw crest was more prominent and much larger.
Its spine featured specialized fusions for stability: the first five dorsal vertebrae were joined into a structure called a notarium, while five sacral vertebrae formed a fused synsacrum.
Tropeognathus is considered the largest pterosaur found in the Southern Hemisphere, with an estimated wingspan of about 8.5 meters.

Later scientific analysis revised the maximum estimated wingspan of the large specimen used in media to 8.70 meters, identifying it as the largest known individual pterosaur based on its completeness.
The specimen MN 6594-V stands out as the largest relatively complete pterosaur individual known to science.
The genus Tropeognathus was described by Peter Wellnhofer in 1987, who named the type species Tropeognathus mesembrinus that same year.
Fossils were found in the Romualdo Formation within the Santana Group in northeastern Brazil, specifically in the Romualdo Member of the Santana Formation.
The holotype specimen BSP 1987 I 46 dates to the latest Aptian and earliest Albian stages; the genus name comes from the Greek words for keel and jaw, while the species name means 'from the south'.
In 2013, Alexander Kellner referred specimen MN 6594-1, a nearly complete skeleton, to Tropeognathus, a conclusion supported by Taissa Rodrigues and Kellner who concluded the genus was valid.
Tropeognathus mesembrinus could have reached a wingspan of around 8.2 meters.
Tropeognathus is classified within the family Anhangueridae, though some studies place it in Ornithocheiridae, a group also known as Anhangueridae.
Recent analyses in 2019 and 2020 place Tropeognathus in the subfamily Tropeognathinae within Anhangueridae, as a sister taxon to Siroccopteryx.
The animal was a close relative of the species in the genus Anhanguera.
Fossils of Tropeognathus date to the Early Cretaceous period, specifically the Albian stage, when the animal lived in South America during the late Early Cretaceous.
Tropeognathus lived between 119.57 and 113.2 million years ago during the Aptian stage.

Researchers have debated the validity of Tropeognathus, often reassigning its fossils to other genera like Anhanguera or Ornithocheirus, but in 2013 researchers concluded that Tropeognathus is a valid genus containing only the species T. mesembrinus.
There is a debate regarding family classification, with some European researchers preferring to place Tropeognathus in Ornithocheiridae rather than Anhangueridae.
